# Using ISLA {#sec-using}

**ISLA ships as one class with one reference configuration, trained and
evaluated by the unified external-aerodynamics recipe; this chapter is the
operating manual.** It tells you which configuration to run and what the
few remaining options are for, what the model needs from your data, the
commands that train and evaluate it, how to set the learning rate when you
change the width or depth, the inference sampler that removes most of the
draw noise at a fixed cell budget, how to load a checkpoint, and what a step
costs. Everything here is about ISLA unless an option is named; the reasons
behind each recommendation are in @sec-isla and the evidence chapters,
cited at the point where they apply.

```{python}
#| label: setup-using
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
import json
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
```

## Which configuration {#sec-using-config}

**Run ISLA as the class ships it: cosine routing, the RMS-pairwise-distance
length unit, the fused geometry kernel where it can run, and interior
queries carrying a share of the total boundary measure.** Those are the
class defaults, so `ISLA()` with no arguments is the reference
configuration; the recipe's `isla_surface.yaml` fixes the dimensions and
states the frame setting explicitly:

```yaml
model:
  _target_: physicsnemo.experimental.nn.ISLA
  out_scalars: 1        # pressure
  out_vectors: 1        # wall shear stress
  hidden: 192
  n_layers: 12
  n_slices: 256
  mlp_ratio: 4
  scale_mode: rms_distance    # length unit = measure-weighted RMS pairwise distance of the sample (the frame has no origin)
  geo_kernel: null            # automatic: the fused Triton kernel on CUDA with one global vector, the eager region otherwise
```

The recipe's width is 192 with 12 layers and 256 slices; this is the one
place the book states it, and the width and depth ladders of
@sec-review-frontier are deviations from it. ISLA has one frame and one
routing form; the rows below are the options that remain on it.

| configuration | recipe config | when to use | what you give up |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ISLA** (cosine routing, RMS-pairwise-distance length unit, fused geometry kernel, `query_mass: source_total`) | `isla_surface`, `isla_volume` | every new surface or interior task | nothing among ISLA's options; the standing against GeoTransolver and Transolver, dataset by dataset and task by task, is in @sec-surface and @sec-interior |
| query mass `geometric_mean` (`query_mass: geometric_mean`) | option on `isla_volume`, `isla_volume_support` | interior tasks only, when a boundary is guaranteed to arrive at one fixed refinement | the refinement contract: each query's routing weight becomes the mean boundary log-weight plus a learned offset, so re-representing the same surface on finer cells shifts the balance between surface and queries (@sec-isla-contracts) |
| passive decoder (`query_independent: true`) | `isla_volume_support` | when the prediction at a point must not depend on which other points are queried | accuracy: a multiple of the interacting decode's error (@sec-interior-query-independence) |
| support tokens (`support_tokens: true`, with the passive decoder) | `isla_volume_support` | when the passive decoder is wanted and a per-case interior support set is available | the extra tokens' cost; the independence contract is kept, because the requested queries are still decoded passively (@sec-arch-modes) |

Every checkpoint stores its constructor arguments, so a model saved under
any option loads in the configuration that trained it (@sec-using-checkpoint).

## What the model needs from your data {#sec-using-inputs}

**ISLA takes four arrays per case, and the two that are easy to get wrong
are the measure weights, which must sum to the boundary's measure, and the
global vectors, which must be directions.** The forward call is
keyword-only, so the recipe's `forward_kwargs:` mapping reads exactly as the
call does. For the surface task:

```yaml
forward_kwargs:
  points: interior.points                                  # (B, N, 3) sampled cell centroids ("interior" is the datapipe's name for the sampled point set, not the fluid domain)
  normals: boundaries.vehicle.cell_data.normals            # (B, N, 3) unit outward normals
  measure_weights: interior.point_data._effective_measure   # (B, N) area each sampled cell stands for
  global_vectors: global_data.U_inf_dir                    # (B, 1, 3) the one global direction of external aerodynamics
```

Three of these need a word.

- **The measure weights must sum to the boundary's measure.** When the
  recipe keeps $n$ of $N$ cells, each kept cell carries the Horvitz–Thompson
  weight, its area times $N/n$, so that the weights stand for the full
  surface at any `sampling_resolution`: the routing's quadrature sums then
  read the surface area rather than the retained fraction of it (the length
  unit normalizes the weights and is indifferent to the factor, but the
  quadrature sums are not). The surface dataset stores this in
  `interior.point_data._effective_measure`; the volume dataset uses
  `boundaries.vehicle.cell_data._effective_measure` through its
  `ComposeQuadratureMeasure` stage. Both are complete measures, including
  sampling corrections. Point measures carry their represented dimension
  and follow geometric scaling: on a two-dimensional problem such as
  AirfRANS the measure is the segment length.
- **A global vector is a direction.** The problem's global directions
  (`n_global_vectors` of them) enter as unit vectors; the model normalizes
  each again internally and discards its magnitude. For external
  aerodynamics `ComputeFreestreamDirection` writes `U_inf_dir` from the
  solver's velocity. This is also the fair-comparison rule for every
  architecture in the book (@sec-unit-direction-rule).
- **A magnitude that matters is a global scalar.** Set `n_global_scalars`
  and pass `global_scalars` of shape (B, S). No fixed power of a far-field
  speed is a physical law for every output (a pressure coefficient is degree
  zero, a dimensional pressure degree two), so the model learns the
  dependence like any other parameter. The AirfRANS configuration passes
  the inlet speed this way (`global_data.U_inf_mag`, $S = 1$).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Problems other than external aerodynamics"}
The architecture knows only that it was handed $K$ global directions and
$S$ global scalars. A buoyant flow passes gravity as its one direction; a
magnetized flow passes two; steady conduction with pinned temperatures
passes none (`n_global_vectors: 0`) and supplies the pinned values as
per-cell `boundary_scalars` (`n_boundary_scalars`). Each global direction
adds one seed cosine, one relational cosine and three vectors to the output
basis (@sec-isla-inputs). The tests in `test_isla_global_inputs.py` cover
zero and two directions, global scalars, and the invariance of the output to
the magnitude of every global vector. The fused geometry kernel is written
for exactly one global direction; with any other count `geo_kernel: null`
resolves to the eager region.
:::

## Training {#sec-using-train}

**Train at the recipe defaults, 200,000 sampled cells per case for 500
epochs at learning rate 1e-3, with no augmentation; the only setting that
needs thought is the learning rate when you leave width 192.** From the
recipe root:

```bash
# DrivAerML Surface task (sampling_resolution defaults to 200,000 cells per case).
# compile=false is the configuration of the evidence lanes; the compiled path computes the same function faster.
python src/train.py model=isla_surface dataset=drivaer_ml_surface \
    training.optimizer.lr=1e-3 compile=false

# DrivAerML Volume task: boundary -> interior, queries as interacting tokens with the signed distance.
python src/train.py model=isla_volume dataset=drivaer_ml_volume_reference \
    training.optimizer.lr=1e-3 compile=false

# HiLiftAeroML surface (the 200,000-cell default again; 500 epochs, as on the cars)
python src/train.py model=isla_surface dataset=highlift_surface \
    training.optimizer.lr=1e-3 compile=false training.num_epochs=500
```

These commands are the reporting protocol of @sec-protocol. ISLA needs no
rotation augmentation: the contracts make it exact, and a model trained in
the dataset's native frame predicts a body in any pose (@sec-pose).

### The learning rate {#sec-using-lr}

**Use 1e-3 at width 192 and 12 layers; for a wider or deeper model, start
from $10^{-3} \times 192 / \mathrm{hidden} \times 12 / \mathrm{layers}$ and
treat it as a starting rate, not a limit.** The expression gives
$5 \times 10^{-4}$ at width 384, $2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ at 768, and
$2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ at 384 wide and 24 layers. It is the rate at which
every width and depth in the capacity ladders trains cleanly, and the
ladders of @sec-review-frontier run at it, so a model trained at the rule
rate is comparable with the book's lanes. Under ISLA's cosine routing the
logits are bounded and the routing-collapse failure that would otherwise
set a hard ceiling on the rate is unreachable (@sec-isla-routing-forms), so
a higher rate is an experiment, not a hazard, and the recipe's ISLA
configurations pin 1e-3 rather than inheriting the recipe-wide default. On
both interior tasks ISLA trains at 1e-3 (@sec-interior).

## Evaluation and the inference sampler {#sec-using-sampler}

**Score in float32 at the reporting protocol's 200,000 cells; when the cell
budget is fixed and smaller, draw the cells with the stratified sampler.**
Inference shares the training configuration and reads the checkpoint by run
identifier:

```bash
# sampling_resolution=200000 is the reporting protocol; the infer default is the whole mesh
python src/infer.py model=isla_surface dataset=drivaer_ml_surface \
    run_id=<the trained run_id> infer_split=val sampling_resolution=200000 precision=float32
```

Report in float32. The recipe trains under bf16 autocast, and every number
in this book is a float32 inference on the final-epoch checkpoint
(@sec-metrics). A bf16 inference differs from the float32 one by rounding
of order a percent, and under a rigid motion of the input its prediction
moves by several percent where the float32 prediction moves at the level of
float32 roundoff (the residuals are tabulated in @sec-isla-contracts).
Where the pose or the sampling-consistency contract is load-bearing, infer
in float32.

**For inference at a fixed cell budget, draw the cells with the stratified
sampler.** Replace the dataset's `SubsampleMesh` stage with the recipe's
`StratifiedSubsampleMesh`:

```yaml
    - _target_: ${dp:StratifiedSubsampleMesh}   # in place of SubsampleMesh
      n_cells: ${sampling_resolution}
```

It keeps the same inclusion law (every cell kept with probability $n/N$,
weight $N/n$), so nothing about the trained model or the quantity it
estimates changes, but the kept cells are a *systematic* draw along the
Morton order of the cell centroids (the ordering by interleaved coordinate
bits, a space-filling curve along which consecutive cells are spatial
neighbors), one per consecutive run of $N/n$ cells with a single random
offset. A systematic sample has the same expectation as an independent draw
for every cell-weighted integral and a lower variance for smooth
integrands. The effect is a free improvement for every model and largest
for ISLA, whose slice states are the noisiest estimates
(@sec-deficit-anatomy).

The book keeps the independent draw for its headline comparisons; for a
deployment, use the stratified draw, or more cells.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="How many cells"}
Use 200,000; error is flat above 100,000 (@sec-equal-budget). If the
budget forces fewer cells, use the stratified draw.
:::

## Loading a trained model {#sec-using-checkpoint}

**A checkpoint carries its own constructor arguments, so loading is one
call and the forward call mirrors the recipe mapping.** A saved ISLA is a
PhysicsNeMo module checkpoint and loads with the class's `from_checkpoint`;
no configuration has to be repeated:

```python
from physicsnemo.experimental.nn import ISLA
model = ISLA.from_checkpoint("checkpoints/isla_surface.mdlus").eval()
out = model(points=x, normals=n, measure_weights=w, global_vectors=g_hat)  # (B, N, 1 + 3)
p, tau = out[..., :1], out[..., 1:]
```

`points` and `normals` are (B, N, 3), `measure_weights` (B, N) summing to the
boundary's measure, `global_vectors` (B, K, 3) or (B, 3) for one direction,
`global_scalars` (B, S) when the model has any. The output stacks the scalar
fields first, then each vector field's three components. For interior
prediction with `isla_volume`, add `query_points`, `query_normals` (the
signed-distance gradient) and `query_scalars` (the signed distance) and read
the output at the query rows; deploy at the training query count (200,000
at the reporting protocol on DrivAerML), because the interacting decode's
prediction at a point depends on the joint query set
(@sec-interior-companion).

## Cost {#sec-using-cost}


**At matched parameter count and the reporting protocol of 200,000 cells
per case, ISLA trains in about a third of GeoTransolver's peak memory and
GPU-floor step time.** @tbl-isla-cost reads both footprints from the
protocol lanes' own training logs. The step is memory-bound at every stage
but the MLP; the per-slice geometry (separations, invariants, routing
softmaxes) is most of the stored activations, which is why the eager path
rebuilds it in the backward pass instead of storing it (`geo_checkpoint`,
bitwise identical outputs and gradients) and why a fused Triton kernel
exists for the geometry region. The kernel is the automatic choice wherever
it can run (CUDA, one global direction, at most 1,024 slices):
`geo_kernel: null` resolves to it at the first forward pass and to the eager
recompute region elsewhere (@sec-arch-switches). Every path computes the
same function (output relative L2 against the eager reference at most
$5.5 \times 10^{-7}$ in bf16, @sec-nb-geokernel-auto). That footprint is
what buys accuracy at scale: on the DrivAerML Surface task at 435 cars,
ISLA reaches GeoTransolver's floor at less than a third of the memory
(@sec-shared-floor).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-isla-cost
#| output: asis
ISO = json.load(open(RES / "isocost_reduction_2026-09-20.json"))["configurations"]
rows = [("ISLA, 192 wide, 1e-3", "isla|w192|c200k|lr1e-3|ep500"), ("GeoTransolver, 256 wide, 3e-3", "gt_unit|w256|c200k|lr3e-3|ep500")]
out = "| architecture | parameters | peak memory per device [GB] | GPU-floor step, p10 [s] | median step [s] |\n|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|\n"
for lab, k in rows:
    c = ISO[k]
    out += f"| {lab} | {c['params']/1e6:.1f}M | {c['peak_mem_gb']:.0f} | {c['step_s_p10']:.2f} | {c['step_s_median']:.2f} |\n"
i, g = ISO[rows[0][1]], ISO[rows[1][1]]
out += f"| GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA | {g['params']/i['params']:.2f}x | {g['peak_mem_gb']/i['peak_mem_gb']:.1f}x | {g['step_s_p10']/i['step_s_p10']:.1f}x | {g['step_s_median']/i['step_s_median']:.1f}x |\n"
print(out)
print(": Training cost at the reporting protocol on the DrivAerML Surface task: 435 cars, 200,000 sampled cells per case, 500 epochs, bfloat16 autocast, one case per "
      "step on one GB300, both models as the recipe trains them (`compile=false`, ISLA on the eager geometry region with the recompute on). Memory is the peak of the logged "
      "per-step values; the GPU-floor step is the tenth percentile of the logged steps (the network alone) and the median is the wall clock a "
      "user waits, which the input pipeline sets at these sizes. How to read this: the table states cost, not accuracy (the standing of these lanes is in @sec-surface); "
      "the ratio row is GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA; it does not show Transolver, whose 200,000-cell cost is not logged, nor the compiled or fused-kernel "
      "paths, which compute the same function faster. Every scored lane of the cost grid is in @tbl-equal-budget. "
      "Data: results/isocost_reduction_2026-09-20.json. {#tbl-isla-cost}")
```

Two practical consequences:

- **Leave `geo_kernel` at its default (`null`).** On CUDA with one global
  direction the model selects the fused kernel at the first forward pass and
  logs the choice; off CUDA, or with several global directions, it falls
  back to the eager recompute region. Force `eager` only to reproduce the
  exact arithmetic path of a checkpoint trained on the eager region.
- **On the eager path, leave `geo_checkpoint: true` unless you are short
  of time and long on memory.** It is bitwise identical in outputs and
  gradients; under the fused kernel the recompute is built in and the flag
  has no effect.

## Contracts you can check on your own data {#sec-using-contracts}

**Each contract is a one-line test on a loaded checkpoint, and a residual
far above float32 rounding points at the inputs, not the model.** The
contracts are exact properties of the code (@sec-isla-contracts), and each
is cheap to verify on a loaded checkpoint: rotate and translate the inputs
by a random rigid motion and compare the scalars (unchanged) and the
vectors (rotated); scale the points by $k$ and the measure weights by $k^2$
(unchanged); scale the measure weights alone (unchanged). In float32 the
residuals on the trained checkpoints are at the level of float32 roundoff;
in bf16 autocast they are several percent, mostly rounding
(@sec-isla-contracts). A residual far above these on your own data means
the inputs, not the model: normals with inconsistent orientation, weights
that do not sum to the boundary's measure, or positions that were already
centered or scaled by something sample-dependent before the model saw them.
(The model normalizes the normals and the global vectors itself, so their
magnitudes cannot cause a residual.)
